Notes: Location of Brockbridge certain, but whether this was the 'Bradebrigge' uncertain.
Newsham Abbey had holdings in the parish (PNLi ii, 218).
HaPNs notes 'Robert Achard', a juror in 1248, and suggests the name was of French origin, or less likely OE ?cheard.

The bridge was the meeting place of the wapentake; in 1286 (YI) an inquisition and in 1324 an execution was held there (PNYoW). The bridge crossed a stream called 'Aggebriggebrook' (also known as Oakenshaw Beck), an alternative name for the settlement.
Possibly a causeway.
Meeting place not known (KePNs; Cullen).

Axbridge is now a far from the Axe and the bridge may be a causeway crossing the Axe levels; the River Brue previously flowed to join with the Axe east of Axbridge, making the crossing point more strategically important than it now appears (Haslam 2014).

A late name.  Bembridge is situated on a peninsula linked by a bridge at Yarbridge built c. 1300 (WtPNs). (Yarbridge was 'Yarnbrigge' 1462, and 'Yarneford' 1324; WtK?.) Probably known as 'Orham' in 1086 (WtPNs; see below).
17th c. forms 'Borna brigghill' and 'Bornabrigg Hill' may be later reflexes of the name, but the development is unusual (PNLi).
Earlier bridge destroyed 1199.
First element a place-name 'Beofanhorn' 'Beofa's corner of land' (PNSx). Bevern now the stream name.
Charter boundary clause evidence.
Bridge repaired in 1224. Formerly Biddenham, also known as Bromham Bridge.
Near Northampton, with a mention of tolls collected.
On the Old North Road/Ermine Street, with toll collection mentioned.
Church apparently originally dedicated to St Botolph, patron saint of wayfarers (PNBdHu).
Construction funded by Queen Matilda (1100-18). An approach road between Bow and London was probably built around the same time.

Notes: OE 'brycg', varying with ON 'bryggja' (PNLi; CDEPN 76). First element uncertain, Mills suggests a variation on OFrench 'brace[ 'arch, support', referring to the structure of the bridge and Coates ON a nominal use of ON 'brattr' 'steep'.
Two bridges mentioned in the twelfth century across both the Colne and the Calder rivers.
Apparently in the thirteenth century this was a timber bridge located to the west of the stone Bramber Bridge.
One of two bridges by Bramber.

PNWo interprets first element as OE 'br?d' 'broad', CDEPN thinks oe 'bred' 'board' more likely, with later reinterpretation as OE 'br?d'. There are several crossings that migth be the referrent.  The church is used as the grid reference here.
Modern canalisation and name of the waterway.
Where Nail Bourne crosses Watling St (M1a) (KePNs; CDEPN).
Land there called 'le Liliclos' (Selby ii, 29 and 35).  There's a 'Lilly Wood' at SE 79664 37577.
Probably preserving name of manor(s) called 'Brige' in DB; perhaps used of a crossing to Portland near Small Mouth: Leyland describes a causeway there in 16th c. (PNDo).
NB Parish includes land north and south of Wye. See Noble for possible survival of Roman bridge at SO 44224 41231.
Personal name Hroaldr that of 1086 holder.

Roman road runs down west of parish crossing River Thet at TL 94088 84080; another route crosses River Thet at TL 98896 86683 in east of parish. However, neither is close to the present settlement and it therefore impossible to decide which of the crossings the name referred to (if it did not refer to an unidentified crossing nearer the village).
A Cuatbrucge recorded in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle (A, s.a. 895) may refer to a bridge at Bridgnorth, in which case a bridge was in existence by teh 9th century. See PNSa (i, 56?59).
Part of the fee of Walter of Douai, said to have built a bridge across the Parrett (CDEPN).
Formerly the Glanford Bridge. First element influenced by ON cognate 'glaumr' (PNLi). Glanford Brigg (brycg/bryggja) in 1235.
Now a modern drain.
Remains of girder bridge over Hull found near Brigham.
The Brig- form is due to ON influence by sound substitution, and is not from a ON 'bryggja' 'quay, jetty'; this was an ancient crossing of the River Calder (PNYoW).
Bridge suggested to be that over Waithe Beck by PNLi.

This is the location of Bristol Bridge which the survey volume suggests might have been the original bridge site. Several more occurences in eleventh century as a mint signature. Stone bridge in existence in 1215.
Development may be due to folk etymological reinterpretation, brushwood being frequently used for causeways.

Original form must have been Bridgeford, i.e. ford with some kind of causeway laid across it; later, perhaps owing to the frequent use of brushwood causeways (cf. Rice Bridge, PN Sx 258), folk- etymology seems to have been at work (PNDe).
Discussion: H. Rye, 'The Great Bridge of Burton-on-Trent', Burton-on-Trent Natural History and Archaeological Society, 5.1 (1903), 4-21.
Uncertain date.
HaPNs notes a William 'le But' in the parish in 1327 and suggests the first element refers to one of his ancestors.
Magdalen Bridge, formerly the Great Bridge. Attested in a 9th-century manuscript of the Life of St Guthlac, thought to have been written in the 8th century
Placename evidence for a bridge.
Repaired in 1256.
A ferry was also in operation. Reading had become the main settlement west of London by ninth to tenth centuries, being well located at the conjunction of the Thames and the Kennet.
Butforth Lane doesn't now cross a watercourse.
Location may not be accurate for 12th c. name.
Presumably located somewhere along the Dean Brook, i.e. the northern bounday of the parish. PNWo is not sure that the valley is well-marked enought to be a 'denu'.
PNLi does not link the Latin and English forms below.
Place-name (English) Bicknor; parish enormous so unclear where this is.
Old Dee Bridge. Domesday Book mentions the bridge was being repaired in the eleventh century.
First element (a shortned form of) Roman 'Corstopitum', with dissimiation of /r - r/ to /l - r/ in some forms. Originally Roman bridge at NY 98017 64624, place-name attested c. 1040.
PNWo suggests this is a reference to a bridge.
Charter boundary clause evidence.

Sapwood dendrochronologically dated to 693 but bridge could have been built later using mature wood (Baker and Brookes 2013). Discussion: C. Salisbury, 'An 8th-Century Mercian Bridge over the Trent at Cromwell, Nottinghamshire, England', Antiquity 69 (1995):1015?18

Gover thinks this is 'bridge by a 'cweorn' or hand mill'; Coates, seeing a genitive plural, thinks this unlikely, and suggests 'bridge [made] of quernstones', but only tentatively. CDEPN suggests 'bridge made or supported by quernstones'.

Notes: Near Ducklington.
In the 1230s the men of Doncaster received permission to collect a toll on their bridge for the purposes of rebuilding it in stone.
Called Dubridge in Domesday Book.
The first stone bridge in Durham was the Old Bridge, built by the bishop. The Elvet Bridge (coordinates used) was erected in 1153x95.
Probably 'Guildsmens bridge'.
On the stream flowing from Itchel House, but lack of <l> in earliest spellings means derivation from this name uncertain.

Must have replaced the ancient ford at early date. Settlement at SK 69137 43136, with grid ref to Gunthorpe Bridge (EW). Affix distinguishes it from West Bridgford at SK 58129 38236 (Trent Bridge), SK 58717 37500 (settlement), in Newark South Division.

Baron identifies with Bridge Fm in Dunwich, but Bridge in Blythburghis also a possibility. At Eastbridge is a crossing over the Minsmere River, although 'the plural DB form may indicated the existence of more than one crossing' (SfPNs 46).
On Ryknild Street, repaired in 1256.
Jervoise identifies six bridges over the Wey with an identical design. He suggests they were all constructed after the 1233 flood when many bridges in the district were damaged.
North and south of the River Crouch.

Ekwall suggests ON compound he translates as 'plank bridge' (DEPN 177), but PNNf points out that ON 'bryggja' was not used itself of a bridge, but normally denoted a jetty/quay. Hybrid name, with the second element influenced from OE 'brycg'? (Mills 187)
This may survive as the TA names Fieldgates, Field Gates Piece (ER).
A very important bridge on the Old North Road/Ermine Street, with toll collection. The bridge was there by the end of the twelfth century. Called 'Ferie' in Domesday Book of 1086.
Hundred name. Two names: OE 'ford' and OE 'fordingabrycg' 'bridge of the dwellers by the ford' (HaPNs). In 1252 pontage was granted for the repair of the bridge.
Two bridges. The first was certainly built c. 1147, and a second one to the west was probably constructed in the thirteenth century.

Place_name: Fredebrvge H' et dim', H' et dim' de Fredrebruge, H' de Fridrebruge, Fredreburge  H' et dim', H' et dim' de Fredrebruga, Fridebruge H'
Notes: First element may be a personal name ON 'Fr??i' or perhaps OE 'fri?, freo?u' 'refuge, protection'. Anderson (EHNs) wonders about OE 'fyrh?' 'a wood' and notes Frith Fields in Tilney All Saints.
No evidence to indicate which bridge the forms refer to (PNLi).
There were probabably several bridges in existence by this date. A charter in 1220 grants land "between the bridges of Gloucester".
'The ford with a (foot-)bridge' or 'by a bridge' (CDEPN).
A collection of small settlements on the outskirts of Rochford.
1st element unglossed in PNLi.
Alternatively OE 'haga' 'enclosure, hedge' in genitive plural 'hagena' (SfPNs).
HaPNs suggests alternatively an '-ingas' name, but this seems unnecessary given the infrequency of forms with medial <-ing->.

The bridge across Hebden water'.  Narrow bridge crossing the river at the upper end of Bridge Gate (PNYoW). Main variants Hepton and Hebden due respectively to progressive and retrogressive assimilation to the unvoiced /p/ and the voiced /d/ (PNYoW).

Probably already in the eight century. For discussion on twelfth century bridge: J. Hillaby, 'Bishop Richard de Capella and the foundation of Herefordshire's market towns' in Essays in honour of Jim and Muriel Tonkin, ed. R. Lowe (Hereford, 2011).

River: modern South Forty Foot Drain / Hammond Beck
Notes: Long embanked road from Donnington to Bridge End, enroute from Nottingham/Grantham to Boston. Mentioned in the 'History of William Marshall'.

Uncertain, forms varied.  The second element seems to be OE/ON 'brycg/bryggja' in all but one form, which is amongst the earliest but contemporaneous with a 'brycg/bryggja' form. Coates (2009, 94) notes that OE '-burh' cannot be excluded as the generic.
Uncertain date, but the bridge was certainly in existence by mid-thirteenth century.
'Bridge of the servants'. 'The bridge was probably on the R. Roden, between Isombridge and Allscott' (PNSh i ).
Have used crossing between church and manor house here; alternatively  perhaps TF 21208 95852, where the surviving road to Brookenby now crosses the river.
This is location of Kettlebridge Lane today.

Location as given in PNWi. OE 'cyne' 'royal' replaced by 'cyning' 'king' in later forms (EHNs).
LdnPNs notes reference to a guild of 'cnihtas' in 11th c. London. Crossing of Westbourne Stream.
OE 'cniht' in genitive plural.
Skerton Bridge repaired in 1216.

To' part of prepostion 'into' (PNGl). PNGL, citing Rudder, notes this may refer to bridge over Severn between Highnam and Gloucester; PNGl suggests Over Causeway, a lengthy causeway. If so 'brycg' means 'hard, raised track through marshland' (PNGl).
Possibly confused with bridge at Twyford; see discussion in Jervoise.
Excavated at Fleet Valley between the Blackfrriars and Holborn viaduct stations.
Rebuild from 1176.

Hundred name. HaPNs suggests personal name Mann. Compare, however, 'Maneshou 1086', for which Parsons (2006, 169) suggests OE 'mann' 'a person' (and compares OE 'ge-m??nnes' 'community').

OE 'r?sn' probably denotes a plank bridge or planks laid across marshy ground. Grid reference given for Church Bridge on George St by be the older, more central road. Alternatively Jameson Bridge to the east of the settlement.

Uncertain date, possibly after 1250.
Probably the Trent Bridge (i.e. the bridge by the castle).
The old bridge, built perhaps on top of Roman foundations, was burnt in 1248 and rebuilt in the 1250s. There was a 'bretasche' (defensive structure) on the bridge in 1219-20.
The most important crossing of the Trent in the 11th century, and a hub of the East Midlands road system.
Headform from 1890s OS (not shown on 1870s OS). First element is the place-name Ower.
Called the Grandpont.
Alternative suggestions the OE personal name '*P?gna' (cf. Paignton) or OE 'penna' (gen. pl. of 'penn 'a pen') fit less well (CDEPN).

Probably a Roman bridge, also refered to in the Assize Rolls of 1243. Or alternatively a causeway across marshy ground rather than the Tees, 'Osier bridge or causeway' (DEPN; DuPNs; CDEPN). (NbDuPNs had taken the specific as the personal name Piers.)

Broken bridge'. In DB known as 'Tateshale' (later Tanshelf), and (perhaps later) the place may have been known as 'Kirkebi'. Both Latin and French origins. Early spellings <Puntfreit , Pontfreit , Pountfreit> etc., are from Old French, Anglo-Norman  'pont(e) freit'.

Place-name Habrough. Localised according to information that bridge was 'between Stallingburgh and Habrough marshes' (see early forms), although it is possible that the forms refer to more than one bridge.
Possibly a reference to a bridge at Bridgnorth, the location of the bruidge in 1100.
Charter boundary clause evidence.
Carrying ancestor or A35 over Test; there are still reeds here (HaCoates).

In the northeast of Barnardiston parish was  an area known as 'Monks Risbridge'. Anderson suggests the name referred to a crossing of a small stream on the southern boundary of this area (if I understand him correctly) (EHNs). Location from SfPNs.
The paved Roman Watling Street was still extant here in 1820.

Attested: Roman, medieval wooden bridge since at least 11thC
Notes: Roman foundations probably used for a bridge at least from the 9th c. onwards, and the bridge was repaired in the early eleventh century.
HaPNs notes absence of medial <e> seems to rule out OE 'r?m' 'spacious' or 'hruna' 'tree trunk' as the specific, and suggests instead OE 'r?n' 'council'. DEPN accepts 'hruna' as a possibility.
The stone bridge (originally Ayleswade, later Harnham Bridge) was built in 1245 by Bishop Bingham. Other structures may have predated it.
The DB form makes it almost certain that the first element is the OE  'sealh' 'willow', and it is on the border of Willoughby (i.e. 'Willow-tree settlement' or 'willow-tree ring').

PNYoE compares 'Skelwislandes' (1318, YD vi), a lost place in Yapham, and Scallow, Sx ('Scalewebregg(e)', 1385 and later forms; PNSx, 401).  The occurrence twice with OE 'brycg' 'bridge' is taken by PNYoE to indicate a meaningful word rather than a personal name.

Coates notes K?keritz's suggestion that Shide (Wi) might mean 'footbridge', and thinks this would be appropriate in this parish, where the Roman road M 420 crossed four minor streams.  He notes OE 'scydd' 'shed' as a less likely possibility.
It is thought that OE 'sc?d', whose meanings include 'board, plank', might have been used of a footbridge here (where the river is fairly narow) (WtK?).

Charter reference to two bridges, presumably the English and Welsh bridges. Both English and Welsh Bridges are mentioned in a charter or King Henry I of 1228. The coordinates are for the English bridge.
Charter reference to two bridges, presumably the English and Welsh bridges. Both English and Welsh Bridges are mentioned in a charter of King Henry I in 1228.
OE 'brycg' may here refer to a bridge over one of the streams here or a causeway across a muddy spot (PNGl).

Either OE '*socabred' ?board serving as a footbridge over marshy spots' (DEPN) or a compound of ME 'soc' ?ploughshare? (< OE 's?cn' ?jurisdiction, estate? or Old French 'soc' ?ploughshare?) and ME brede (< OE 'br?du') 'broad cultivated strip, furrow' (PNWe).
A bridge existed in 1315, when the township of Sowerby was fined for not repairing it. May have replaced 'Sowerby ford'.
Uncertain date, but the bridge was certainly in existence by mid-thirteenth century.

Bridge built on posts or piles'. The name may refer to a bridge over the Stour or Bibbern Brook (PNDo, citing Penn). Alternative at ST 74504 17236 or ST 76464 19024.
On the Old North Road/Ermine Street.
Refers to crossing of Derwent by Roman road here (PNYoE).
PNBdHu suggests village took name from bridge at Stanbridgeford a mile to the south-east. Half-hundred named from Stanbridge; location just below Totternhoe.
Two manors and a deserted medieval village (HaCoates). Apparently a bridge over the Test (HaPNs; HaCoates).

The name refers to the bridge over the Lea here. The forms '(de) Ponte Tegule' and 'Punt de Tyulle' recorded form the thirteenth century mean 'tile bridge', and it is possible that this was later confused with '?el' 'plank' for it is very unlikely that the river here could ever have been crossed by a plank bridge (PNHt).
Known as the Kingsbridge in the time of King Henry III (1216?72). It was in disrepair in 1278.

Localised using copy of Enclosure Award Plan (East Riding of Yorkshire Archives, IA/22, parcels 19, 20 and 21).  Parcel 19 is westernmost, so feature may have been on road to Eastrington (SE 81488 30845).

A great causeway from Stuntney and Soham to Ely.

First element apparently to be derived from the Sawin (OE personal name 'S?wine') who held the manor of Birige in 1086 (DB f. 194 b). If this is so, the stress accent must later have been shifted to the second syllable. The bridge here is over a tributary of the Taw.

Generic alternatively OE 'h?m', as 'hamm' is not known to occur elsewhere in Norfolk or Suffolk, with specific a metathesized form of OE '*??felett' 'thicket' (SfPNs).

Deep pool at a plank' probably 'pool with a plank bidge' (PNCh). The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle refers to a burh established here in 922 by Eadward the Elder, presumably to guard the crossing of the Mersey at Latchford. The deep pool would probably be a place in the River Mersey.

Two bridges: the Ouse Bridge (coordinates given) and the Foss Bridge. Rebuilt in stone probably in late twelfth century. The earliest charter evidence is for the Ouse Bridge in 1189x1200 and for the Foss Bridge in 1145x48 (Stell).
